slides.text:
Some code never produces a value: it ends the program, loops forever or jumps somewhere else. Rust gives that kind of expression its own type, `!`, called the never type.

A function that ends this way is a diverging function, and it is written `-> !`.

You will write functions that never return, see why `loop` and `std::process::exit` fit one, and learn the rule that makes `panic!`, `continue` and `unreachable!` fit any type.

`todo!` and `dbg!` are macros, taught in `std-macros-expanded`.

A normal function ends by handing control back to its caller. A function marked `-> !` promises control never comes back: it stops the program or repeats forever.

Its body can never end normally, so it has no final value and no `break` out of its loop.

Pseudo code, not Rust.

exercises.title: A function that never returns
exercises.guide: Write a function that ends the whole program.

chunks.guide: `-> !` means the function never returns. It stops the program with `std::process::exit`.

notes.text: No value ever comes back from this function.
Ends the program at once, with this exit code.

exercises.title: Code after a diverging call
exercises.guide: Read the code, then pick the output.
exercises.explanation: `fail` never returns, so the program ends inside it. The last `println!` can never run; the compiler only warns about unreachable code.

exercises.title: A loop that never ends
exercises.guide: Build a countdown that never returns.

chunks.guide: A `loop` with no `break` never ends, so it fits a `-> !` function. The exit inside is the only way out.

notes.text: No break inside, so it never finishes normally.

exercises.title: Never-ending function
exercises.guide: Fill the return type of a function that never returns, and the statement that repeats forever.

slides.text:
Every branch of an `if` or `match` must give the same type. An expression of type `!` gives no value at all, so Rust lets it stand in for any type.

`return`, `break`, `continue` and `panic!` are all of type `!`. This is how a branch can bail out while the others give a number.

exercises.title: A panic in a match arm
exercises.guide: Pick a port for an environment, and stop on an unknown one.

chunks.guide: Two arms give a `u32`. `panic!` stops the program with a message, and its type `!` fits the last arm.

notes.text: Stops the program with a message; fits any type.

chunks.guide: Both calls use a known environment, so no panic happens.

exercises.title: Skip with continue
exercises.guide: Add up the even numbers, skipping the odd ones from inside a `let`.

chunks.guide: The `if` gives `n` for even numbers. The `else` branch is `continue`, of type `!`, so `even` is always a number.

notes.text: Jumps to the next number; it never gives a value.

exercises.title: Why does it compile?
exercises.guide: The `else` branch has no number. Pick why this is allowed.
options: The else branch is skipped at compile time
panic! gives 0 when the branch types differ
panic! has type !, which fits any type
panic! is converted to u32 at run time
exercises.explanation: `panic!` never produces a value, so its type is `!`, and `!` can stand in for `u32` here. Nothing is skipped or converted.

exercises.title: An arm that cannot run
exercises.guide: Score a number by its remainder, and mark the impossible arm.

chunks.guide: A remainder of 3 is only 0, 1 or 2, but the compiler cannot know that, so `_` is still needed. `unreachable!()` says it can never happen.

notes.text: Panics if ever reached, so it points at a bug.

exercises.title: Skip the unpaid orders
exercises.guide: Orders of 0 are not paid yet. Fill the keyword that jumps to the next order from inside the `else`.
